lesson.menu_title: If I Could Change One Thing

lesson.subtitle: Lesson 4 -- If I Could Change One Thing
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Gustavo Marinho de Carvalho | Lesson 4 -- If I Could Change One Thing

listenings.text: There is one small change that makes a disagreement easier to have, and it is not about being polite. It is about the tense. Compare two sentences. The first one is: that policy is wrong. The second one is: if it were my decision, I would start somewhere else. Both say the same thing, and the second one is far easier to answer, because it puts the idea one step away from the person saying it. The other side can argue with the idea without arguing with you. This is why so much of the language of negotiation and of public argument sits in the hypothetical. It is not weakness and it is not indirectness for its own sake. It is a way of keeping a conversation open long enough for somebody to change their mind, including you.

The most useful question I have ever learned in a professional argument is six words long. What would change your mind here. Not why do you think that, which people hear as an attack, and not are you sure, which they hear as doubt about them. What would change your mind. It asks for the shape of their thinking, not for a defence of their conclusion, and almost nobody has ever been asked it. Two things happen when you do. The first is that they slow down, because they have to think instead of repeat. The second is the one that matters. Sooner or later somebody asks you the same question back, and you find out whether you have an answer. If nothing would change your mind, then what you have is not an opinion. It is a position, and those are much less interesting to talk about.

paras: In February 2003 central London started charging drivers to enter a small area in the middle of the city during working hours. The idea was not new and it was not popular. Shops said they would lose customers, drivers said it was a tax on getting to work, and several newspapers predicted the whole thing would be reversed within a year.

What happened next is why the story is still told. Traffic inside the zone fell, and it stayed lower for years afterwards. The money collected went into public transport. The charge was not reversed. It was extended, and cities in several other countries sent people to London to see how it worked.

None of that makes it a simple success, and the text you are reading is not going to pretend it does. Businesses just outside the zone argued for years that they were carrying a cost they had never agreed to. And the charge is the same for a driver who has a real alternative and for a driver who has none, which is a serious objection and not a small one. Every version of this policy since has had to answer it, and no version has answered it completely.

That is exactly what makes it worth arguing about. There is no side here that has nothing to explain. If you had to design it again from nothing, what would you keep, and what would you refuse to repeat? The question has no correct answer, and it is very close to the kind of question somebody in another country will ask you about your own city.
reading.source: Written for this lesson from public reporting on the London congestion charge, introduced in 2003.
